meta.title: LLM Training: From Pre-training to RLHF
meta.subtitle: A deep dive into how Large Language Models are trained

content.title: The Foundation
content.content: Pre-training is teaching an LLM to predict the next {term:token:token} given previous tokens. It's like teaching a child to read by showing them billions of sentences.

Objective: Learn general language patterns, facts, and reasoning abilities from massive text corpora.

Scale: Trillions of {term:token:tokens}, thousands of GPUs, weeks to months of training.

rows: Web text (Common Crawl), books, Wikipedia, code (GitHub)
Next token prediction (causal LM) or masked LM
Base model that can complete text but isn't instruction-following

explanation.template: Minimize the negative log {term:probability:probability} of predicting the correct next {term:token:token} given all previous tokens. The {term:weights:model weights θ} are updated via {term:gradient:gradient descent}.

content.title: What happens during training?
content.content:
1. Sample a batch of text sequences from {term:data:training data}
2. For each {term:token:token}, compute model's {term:probability:probability distribution} over vocabulary
3. Calculate {term:loss:cross-entropy loss} against ground truth
4. Backpropagate to compute {term:gradient:gradients}
5. Update {term:weights:weights} using optimizer (Adam, AdamW)

content.title: What the model learns
content.content:
• Syntax & Grammar: Proper sentence structure
• World Knowledge: Facts about entities, events, concepts
• Reasoning Patterns: Logical chains, analogies
• Code Understanding: Programming languages, APIs
• Multilinguality: Many languages from diverse web data

content.title: But there's a problem...
content.content:
The base model predicts likely continuations, not helpful responses.

Prompt: 'What is the capital of France?'
Base Model: 'What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Italy?...' (continues the pattern)

We need fine-tuning to make it assistant-like!

content.title: What is SFT?
content.content:
SFT = Teaching the model to follow instructions by showing it (instruction, response) pairs.

Unlike pre-training which uses raw text, SFT uses curated high-quality examples of how an assistant should behave.
Goal: Transform a text completion model into an instruction-following assistant.

content.title: Data Format
content.content:
Input: '[INST] What is machine learning? [/INST]'
Target: 'Machine learning is a subset of AI that enables systems to learn from data...'

The {term:loss:loss} is only computed on the response tokens, not the instruction.

explanation.template: Only the {term:token:tokens} in the response contribute to the {term:loss:loss}. The instruction provides context but isn't predicted.

content.title: Key Techniques
content.content:
• LoRA/QLoRA: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (freeze base, train adapters)
• Instruction Templates: Consistent format for prompts
• Chat Format: Multi-turn conversation structure
• Data Quality: More important than quantity

content.title: What SFT achieves
content.content:
✅ Follows instructions
✅ Answers questions directly
✅ Maintains consistent persona
✅ Formats outputs properly (code, lists, etc.)

content.title: But there are limitations...
content.content:
❌ Imitates, doesn't optimize: Copies annotator behavior, good or bad
❌ Distribution mismatch: May struggle outside training distribution
❌ No preference learning: Doesn't know which of two good answers is better

This is where RLHF comes in!

content.title: What is RLHF?
content.content:
RLHF = Using human preferences to train a {term:reward:reward model}, then optimizing the LLM to maximize that {term:reward:reward} while staying close to the SFT model.

It's teaching the model not just what to say, but how well to say it.

The Three Steps:
1. SFT - Create initial instruction-following model
2. Reward Model - Train model to predict human preferences
3. RL Optimization - Optimize {term:policy:policy} against {term:reward:reward} with {term:kl:KL} constraint

content.title: Why not just use more SFT data?
content.content:
• Human preferences are comparative: 'A is better than B' is easier to annotate than writing perfect responses
• SFT copies behavior; RLHF optimizes for quality
• RLHF learns subtle preferences that are hard to explicitly write down

content.title: The Classic RLHF Algorithm
content.content: PPO is the standard RL algorithm used in RLHF. It updates the {term:policy:policy} to maximize {term:reward:reward} while constraining how much the {term:policy:policy} can change in each step.

explanation.template: Maximize {term:reward:reward} (via {term:advantage:advantage}) while keeping the {term:policy:policy} close to the {term:reference:reference model} using a {term:kl:KL divergence} penalty.

content.title: Key Components
content.content:
• r(θ): Ratio of new to old {term:policy:policy} {term:probability:probabilities}
• {term:advantage:A}: How much better the action is than expected
• clip: Prevents too large updates
• {term:kl:KL} penalty: Prevents model from drifting too far from SFT

content.title: A Simpler Alternative
content.content: GRPO (from DeepSeek) eliminates the need for a separate {term:value:value function} by computing {term:advantage:advantages} relative to a group of samples for the same prompt.

explanation.template: Instead of learning a {term:value:value function}, GRPO samples multiple responses per prompt and uses the group's {term:reward:reward} statistics to compute relative {term:advantage:advantages}.

content.title: Why GRPO is Popular
content.content:
• Simpler implementation (no critic network)
• Used by DeepSeek for their R1 model
• Works well with verifiable rewards (math, code)
• Easier to scale

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Think of {term:loss:loss} as a 'wrongness score'. Like a teacher grading a test - 0 means perfect, higher means more mistakes. The model's goal is to get this as close to 0 as possible.

Cross-entropy {term:loss:loss} measures the negative log-likelihood of the correct {term:token:token}. Formula: {term:loss:L} = −Σ log {term:probability:P}(correct {term:token:token} | context). Lower values indicate the model assigns higher {term:probability:probability} to correct answers.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: Model sees 'The capital of France is ___'
Step 2: Model predicts {term:probability:probabilities} for every word in vocabulary
Step 3: Model assigns 90% to 'Paris' (the correct answer)
Step 4: Calculate {term:loss:L} = −log(0.9) ≈ 0.105
Step 5: Low {term:loss:loss}! Model was confident and correct.

Bad case: If model only gave 10% to 'Paris':
{term:loss:L} = −log(0.1) ≈ 2.3 (high = needs improvement)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Imagine you're blindfolded on a hill trying to reach the bottom (lowest {term:loss:loss}). The {term:gradient:gradient} tells you which direction is steepest downhill. It's your 'compass' for improving the model.

{term:gradient:∇}{term:loss:L} is a vector of partial derivatives of the {term:loss:loss} function with respect to each {term:weights:weight} parameter. It points in the direction of steepest increase, so we move opposite to it.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: Current {term:weights:weights} θ = [2.0, 3.0, 1.5]
Step 2: Compute {term:loss:loss} on a batch of {term:data:data}
Step 3: Calculate {term:gradient:gradient}: {term:gradient:∇}L = [0.1, -0.2, 0.05]
Step 4: Apply learning rate (lr = 0.001):
θ_new = θ − lr × {term:gradient:∇}L
θ_new = [2.0, 3.0, 1.5] − [0.0001, -0.0002, 0.00005]
Step 5: New {term:weights:weights} = [1.9999, 3.0002, 1.49995]
Result: {term:loss:Loss} should be slightly lower now!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: All the numbers inside the neural network that get learned during training. The 'brain' of the model.
{term:weights:θ} ∈ ℝⁿ where n = billions for modern LLMs. Includes embeddings, attention weights, MLP weights, layer norms.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B: 7 billion {term:weights:parameters}
GPT-4: ~1.7 trillion {term:weights:parameters}

Stored as fp16/bf16 floats, so 7B params ≈ 14GB

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Training {term:data:data} is the 'textbooks' the model learns from. Just like a student studying - better books lead to better knowledge. Garbage in = garbage out.

{term:data:D} = {x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ} is the corpus of text sequences. Each xᵢ is tokenized into {term:token:tokens}. The model learns the statistical distribution P(xᵢ) to minimize {term:loss:loss} over {term:data:D}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Pre-training {term:data:data}:
Step 1: Crawl the web (Common Crawl: 250B pages)
Step 2: Add quality sources (Wikipedia, books, GitHub code)
Step 3: Filter out low-quality/harmful content
Step 4: Tokenize into ~2 trillion {term:token:tokens}

SFT {term:data:data}:
Step 1: Human writes instruction: 'Explain quantum physics simply'
Step 2: Human writes ideal response: 'Imagine particles as...'
Step 3: Collect 50K-1M such pairs
Step 4: Model learns to imitate these responses

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A {term:token:token} is a chunk of text that the {term:model:model} actually 'sees'. Words get broken into pieces that exist in the {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. The {term:model:model} doesn't work with text directly - it works with numeric IDs!

{term:token:Tokens} are produced by a tokenizer (BPE, SentencePiece, WordPiece). Each {term:token:token} maps to an integer ID in range [0, {term:vocabulary:vocab_size}). The {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} is fixed during training, typically 32K-100K entries.

sections.title: Visual Example: Word → Token → ID
sections.content:
Input text: 'Hello, world!'

Step 1 - Tokenization:
'Hello' → ['Hello'] → [{term:token:15496}]
',' → [','] → [{term:token:11}]
' world' → [' world'] → [{term:token:995}]
'!' → ['!'] → [{term:token:0}]

Step 2 - What {term:model:model} sees:
[15496, 11, 995, 0] ← Just numbers!

Subword example:
'Unbelievable' → ['Un', 'believ', 'able'] → [{term:token:1525}, {term:token:6975}, {term:token:540}]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A {term:probability:probability distribution} is the {term:model:model}'s 'confidence spread' over ALL possible next {term:token:tokens}. Think of it as betting chips - the {term:model:model} distributes 100% across every word in the {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. Higher % = more confident that's the next word.

{term:probability:P}({term:token:t}|context) = {term:softmax:softmax}({term:logits:logits})[{term:token:t}]. The {term:model:model} outputs raw {term:logits:logits} (one per {term:vocabulary:vocab} entry), then {term:softmax:softmax} converts them to a valid {term:probability:probability} distribution that sums to 1.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The capital of France is'

Step 1: {term:model:Model} outputs {term:logits:logits} for all 50K {term:vocabulary:vocab} entries
Step 2: Apply {term:softmax:softmax} to convert to {term:probability:probabilities}
Step 3: Result:
• {term:probability:P}('Paris') = 0.92
• {term:probability:P}('Lyon') = 0.03
• {term:probability:P}('Berlin') = 0.01
• ...49,996 other {term:token:tokens} share remaining 0.04

{term:summation:Σ} of all {term:probability:probabilities} = 1.0 (always!)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Think of {term:reward:reward} as a 'quality score' or 'star rating' for responses. Like rating restaurant reviews - 5 stars for helpful, accurate answers; 1 star for unhelpful or wrong ones. The model learns to get more stars!

{term:reward:R}: (prompt, response) → ℝ is a scalar function trained on human preference data. Given pairs (response_A, response_B) where humans prefer A, the {term:reward:reward} model learns: {term:reward:R}(A) > {term:reward:R}(B). Training uses Bradley-Terry model with cross-entropy {term:loss:loss}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: User asks: 'Explain gravity to a 5-year-old'
Step 2: Model generates two responses:
• Response A: 'Gravity is like invisible glue that pulls things down...'
• Response B: 'Gravity is the curvature of spacetime caused by mass...'
Step 3: {term:reward:Reward} model scores both:
• {term:reward:R}(A) = 0.85 (appropriate for audience)
• {term:reward:R}(B) = 0.32 (too complex)
Step 4: Model {term:policy:policy} is updated via {term:gradient:gradients} to generate more A-like responses
Result: Model learns to tailor responses to the audience!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:policy:policy} IS the LLM - it's the 'decision maker'. Like a chef deciding what ingredients to add next, the {term:policy:policy} decides what {term:token:token} to generate next. It's the model's 'personality' or 'strategy' for responding.

{term:policy:π_θ}(response|prompt) = ∏ᵢ {term:probability:P}({term:token:tᵢ}|prompt, {term:token:t}<i) where {term:weights:θ} are the model parameters. The {term:policy:policy} defines a distribution over all possible responses.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: User says 'Hi'
Step 2: {term:policy:Policy π} considers possible responses:
• 'Hello!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.05
• 'Hi there!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.12
• 'Hey!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.08
Step 3: During RLHF, we discover 'Hi there!' gets higher {term:reward:reward}
Step 4: Update {term:weights:θ} via {term:gradient:gradient} to increase {term:probability:P}('Hi there!')
Step 5: After training, new {term:policy:policy} might give:
• 'Hi there!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.25 (increased!)
Result: {term:policy:Policy} now favors higher-{term:reward:reward} responses!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:value:value} function is like a 'fortune teller' for {term:reward:rewards}. Given where we are in generating a response, it predicts: 'How good will the final response probably be?' It helps the model know if it's on the right track mid-generation.

{term:value:V}(s) = 𝔼[Σ {term:reward:R}_t | s_0 = s] is the expected cumulative {term:reward:reward} from state s. In RLHF, a separate 'critic' network estimates {term:value:V} to compute {term:advantage:advantages}: {term:advantage:A} = {term:reward:R} - {term:value:V}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: Model is mid-response: 'The answer is...'
Step 2: {term:value:Value} function predicts: 'Based on this start, expected final {term:reward:reward} ≈ 0.6'
Step 3: Model completes: 'The answer is 42'
Step 4: Actual {term:reward:reward} = 0.8
Step 5: {term:advantage:Advantage} = 0.8 - 0.6 = +0.2 (better than expected!)
Step 6: This positive {term:advantage:advantage} encourages similar responses

Note: GRPO eliminates the {term:value:value} function by using group statistics instead!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:kl:KL divergence} measures 'how different' two {term:probability:probability} distributions are. Think of it as a 'drift detector' - it alerts us when the RL-trained model strays too far from the original SFT model. It's like keeping a student on track so they don't learn bad habits while trying to get good grades.

{term:kl:KL}(P||Q) = Σₓ P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)). Properties: Always ≥ 0, equals 0 iff P = Q, asymmetric. In RLHF: {term:kl:KL}({term:policy:π} || {term:reference:π_ref}) penalizes deviation from the SFT baseline.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: {term:reference:Reference} model ({term:reference:π_ref}) probabilities for 'How are you?':
• 'I'm good' → 0.4, 'Fine' → 0.3, 'Great!' → 0.2, 'AMAZING!!!' → 0.1
Step 2: After RL, new {term:policy:policy} ({term:policy:π}) might become:
• 'I'm good' → 0.1, 'AMAZING!!!' → 0.8 (reward hacking!)
Step 3: Calculate {term:kl:KL} divergence:
{term:kl:KL} = 0.1×log(0.1/0.4) + 0.8×log(0.8/0.1) = very high!
Step 4: High {term:kl:KL} penalty reduces total objective
Step 5: Model is pushed back toward natural responses
Result: Prevents 'reward hacking' while still improving!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: How much better an action is compared to the average. Positive = better than expected, negative = worse.
{term:advantage:A}(s,a) = Q(s,a) - {term:value:V}(s). Or in GRPO: normalized {term:reward:reward} within a group.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Group of 4 responses with {term:reward:rewards} [0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.3]
Mean = 0.45, Std = 0.23

{term:advantage:A} for response with R=0.8:
= (0.8 - 0.45) / 0.23 = 1.52 (strongly positive)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:reference:reference policy} is your 'safety copy' - the well-behaved SFT model frozen in time. It's like having a responsible adult supervising a teenager (the RL {term:policy:policy}) who's trying new things. Keeps the model from going off the rails.

{term:reference:π_ref} is a frozen copy of the {term:policy:policy} {term:weights:weights} before RL training begins. The {term:kl:KL} penalty term {term:kl:KL}({term:policy:π}||{term:reference:π_ref}) constrains how far the learned {term:policy:policy} can deviate.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: Start with SFT model → Save copy as {term:reference:π_ref} (frozen)
Step 2: Initialize RL {term:policy:policy} {term:policy:π} = copy of SFT model (trainable)
Step 3: During RL, model learns responding 'ABSOLUTELY FANTASTIC!!!' gets high {term:reward:reward}
Step 4: But {term:reference:π_ref} would say 'I'm doing well, thank you'
Step 5: {term:kl:KL}({term:policy:π}||{term:reference:π_ref}) = HIGH (big difference)
Step 6: High {term:kl:KL} penalty reduces the objective, discouraging this
Result: Model improves but stays grounded in normal language!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} is the {term:model:model}'s complete dictionary - every word piece it knows. Think of it as a numbered list where each entry has an ID. If a word isn't in the {term:vocabulary:vocab}, it gets split into smaller pieces that ARE.

{term:vocabulary:V} = {{term:token:t₀}, {term:token:t₁}, ..., {term:token:t_n}} where |V| is typically 32K-100K. Each {term:token:token} maps to a unique integer ID. The {term:model:model} outputs {term:logits:logits} with shape [|V|], one score per {term:vocabulary:vocab} entry.

sections.title: What Vocabulary Looks Like
sections.content:
Sample entries (GPT-style):
ID 0: '!'
ID 11: ','
ID 262: ' the'
ID 995: ' world'
ID 15496: 'Hello'

Size matters:
• GPT-2: 50,257 entries
• LLaMA: 32,000 entries
• GPT-4: ~100K entries

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:softmax:Softmax} converts raw scores ({term:logits:logits}) into {term:probability:probabilities}. It's like converting test scores into percentages - bigger scores get bigger percentages, and they all add up to 100%.

{term:softmax:softmax}(z)_i = exp(z_i) / {term:summation:Σ}_j exp(z_j). Properties: (1) Output ∈ (0,1), (2) {term:summation:Σ} outputs = 1, (3) Preserves order of inputs, (4) Amplifies differences between values.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: {term:model:Model} outputs {term:logits:logits}: [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]
Step 2: Compute exp: [7.39, 2.72, 1.11]
Step 3: Sum: 7.39 + 2.72 + 1.11 = 11.22
Step 4: Divide each by sum:
• {term:probability:P}_0 = 7.39/11.22 = 0.66
• {term:probability:P}_1 = 2.72/11.22 = 0.24
• {term:probability:P}_2 = 1.11/11.22 = 0.10
Result: [0.66, 0.24, 0.10] - sums to 1.0!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:logits:Logits} are the raw 'scores' the neural network produces before converting to {term:probability:probabilities}. They can be any number (positive, negative, huge). Think of them as the {term:model:model}'s 'pre-grades' before being curved.

{term:logits:Logits} ∈ ℝ^|V| are the output of the final linear layer before {term:softmax:softmax}. Shape: [batch_size, seq_len, {term:vocabulary:vocab_size}]. Higher {term:logits:logit} = {term:model:model} more favors that {term:token:token}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The capital of France is'

Step 1: Text → {term:token:token} IDs → embeddings
Step 2: Pass through transformer layers
Step 3: Final layer outputs {term:logits:logits} for each {term:vocabulary:vocab} entry:
• 'Paris' (ID 6342): {term:logits:logit} = 4.2 (high!)
• 'London' (ID 4712): {term:logits:logit} = 1.1
• 'the' (ID 262): {term:logits:logit} = -2.3
Step 4: Apply {term:softmax:softmax} to get {term:probability:probabilities}

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:model:model} is the entire 'brain' - the neural network that takes input and produces output. It's the combination of architecture (how layers connect) + {term:weights:weights} (learned numbers). Same architecture + different {term:weights:weights} = different {term:model:model}.

A {term:model:model} f_{term:weights:θ}: X → Y is a parameterized function where {term:weights:θ} are learned during training. For LLMs: input = {term:token:token} sequence, output = {term:logits:logits} over {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. Architecture defines the function class; training finds optimal {term:weights:θ}.

sections.title: What's Inside a Model
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B architecture:
• Embedding: {term:vocabulary:vocab} → 4096-dim vectors
• 32 transformer layers, each with:
- Self-attention (Q, K, V projections)
- MLP (feed-forward network)
- Layer normalization
• Final linear: 4096 → {term:vocabulary:vocab_size}

Total: 7 billion {term:weights:parameters} = the learned 'knowledge'

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:summation:Σ} symbol means 'add everything up'. When you see {term:summation:Σ}_i, it means 'for each value of i, compute what's inside, then add all results together'. It's shorthand for a loop that adds.

{term:summation:Σ}_{i=a}^{b} f(i) = f(a) + f(a+1) + ... + f(b). In {term:loss:loss} functions, we sum over all {term:token:tokens} in a sequence. In {term:softmax:softmax}, we sum over all {term:vocabulary:vocab} entries.

sections.title: Examples in LLM Training
sections.content:
In Cross-Entropy {term:loss:Loss}:
{term:loss:L} = -{term:summation:Σ}_{i=1}^{T} log P(t_i)
= -log P(t_1) - log P(t_2) - ... - log P(t_T)
Sum {term:loss:loss} over all T {term:token:tokens}

In {term:softmax:Softmax}:
{term:summation:Σ}_j exp(z_j) = exp(z_1) + exp(z_2) + ...
Sum over all {term:vocabulary:vocab} entries
